questions.prompt: Every green build on main is packaged and could go live, but a release manager presses a button to push it to production. Which practice is this?
options: Continuous integration only, because nothing is deployed until the release manager acts
Continuous delivery, because every build is releasable but the final deploy is manual
Continuous deployment, because the pipeline already produces a production-ready artifact
Blue-green deployment, because a human decides when to switch traffic to the new build
questions.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps every green build releasable and leaves the production push to a human decision. Continuous deployment removes that manual gate.

questions.prompt: Your pipeline builds a fresh container image separately for staging and for production from the same commit. What is the main risk?
options: Production may run bits that differ from what was tested, e.g. a dependency changed between builds
The registry will reject the second push because the commit SHA tag already exists there
Staging will be slower than production because its image is built first in the pipeline
Nothing, because building from the same commit always yields byte-identical images
questions.explanation: Rebuilds can pull different base images or dependency versions, so production runs untested bits. Build once, tag by commit SHA, and promote the same artifact.

questions.prompt: A new recommendation feature is risky and needs a quick kill switch that does not require redeploying. Which approach fits best?
options: A rolling update that replaces two instances at a time across the whole fleet
A longer staging soak period before the change is merged into the main branch
Rebuilding the artifact with the feature removed whenever a problem is detected
Wrap the feature in a feature flag so it can be turned off at runtime instantly
questions.explanation: A feature flag separates deploy from release: the code ships dark and the flag can disable it in seconds without a new build or deploy.

questions.prompt: A suite has 40 browser end-to-end tests, 10 integration tests and 5 unit tests. It takes 50 minutes and fails randomly. What is the best first move?
options: Add more end-to-end tests so that every failure path is covered in a real browser
Push most checks down into fast unit and integration tests, keeping a few key E2E flows
Raise the CI timeout and rerun failed jobs automatically until they eventually pass
Delete the unit tests, since end-to-end tests already exercise the same code paths
questions.explanation: This is the inverted pyramid (ice-cream cone). Moving most checks to unit and integration level makes the suite fast and stable while a few E2E tests cover critical journeys.

questions.prompt: You want to assert that your signup code calls email.send() exactly once with the new user's address. Which test double is designed for this?
options: A stub that returns a canned success value whenever email.send() is called by the code
A dummy object passed in to fill the parameter but never actually used by the code
A mock or spy that records the call so you can verify its count and arguments
A fake in-memory email server that stores messages but is never inspected by the test
questions.explanation: Mocks and spies exist to verify interactions such as call count and arguments. Stubs only feed answers in; dummies are never used.

questions.prompt: A team hits 100% line coverage, yet a bug ships in the else-branch of a validation check. What best explains this?
options: Line coverage counts executed code, not checked behavior; branch coverage or real asserts were missing
100% coverage guarantees correctness, so the bug must come from the production environment instead
The coverage tool double-counted lines, which always happens when tests run in parallel mode
The bug is in a third-party library, because coverage measures only the project's own code
questions.explanation: Coverage shows which code ran, not whether results were asserted, and line coverage can hide untaken branches. Treat it as a map of untested code, not a quality target.

questions.prompt: Your SLO is 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. One incident already caused 30 minutes of full outage. Roughly how much error budget remains?
options: About 413 minutes, since the budget is 1% of the month
None, because any outage breaches a 99.9% objective
About 13 minutes of the 43.2-minute monthly budget
About 43 minutes, since budgets reset after each incident
questions.explanation: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes; 43.2 - 30 leaves about 13 minutes. The team should slow risky releases until the budget recovers.

questions.prompt: Which alert is the best candidate to page an on-call engineer at 3 a.m.?
options: Average CPU on one database replica has stayed above 85% for ten minutes
Disk usage on a log volume crossed 70% and is growing slowly this week
A single pod restarted once after being evicted for scheduling reasons
The checkout SLO is burning error budget fast enough to exhaust it in hours
questions.explanation: Page on symptoms users feel, such as fast SLO burn. Causes like CPU or a single restart belong on dashboards or tickets unless they affect users.

questions.prompt: Checkout p99 latency jumped from 300 ms to 2 s. Which signal most directly shows which downstream service is slow?
options: A distributed trace showing span durations for each service call in the request
The average latency metric across all endpoints aggregated over the past day
Free-text application logs searched for the word 'slow' across all the hosts
The SLA document listing contractual availability targets for checkout traffic
questions.explanation: Traces break one request into timed spans across services, so the slow hop stands out. Averages hide the tail and unstructured logs are hard to correlate.

questions.prompt: terraform plan shows '-/+ aws_db_instance.main must be replaced' after you edited one argument. What should you do before applying?
options: Apply immediately, because replace is just Terraform's word for an in-place update
Stop and check which argument forces replacement, since recreating the database can lose data
Delete the state file so Terraform forgets the database and creates a fresh one cleanly
Run terraform init again, because a replace in the plan means providers are outdated
questions.explanation: -/+ means destroy then create. For stateful resources like databases, find the argument that forces replacement and use a safer change or a lifecycle guard.

questions.prompt: Two engineers run terraform apply at the same time against the same environment, and state gets corrupted. What prevents this?
options: Running terraform fmt before every commit so both configurations stay identical
Keeping a separate local state file on each engineer's laptop for that environment
Pinning provider versions in the required_providers block of the root module
A remote backend with state locking so only one apply can hold the state at a time
questions.explanation: A remote backend with locking serializes writes to state. Local per-laptop state makes conflicts worse, and formatting or version pins do not coordinate runs.

questions.prompt: Someone opened port 22 on a security group in the cloud console. The Terraform code only allows 443. What is this, and how is it usually caught?
options: Drift; a scheduled terraform plan shows the difference between real infra and code
A module version conflict; terraform init -upgrade will report and revert the change
Imperative provisioning; Terraform blocks console changes for managed resources
State locking failure; the lock file records every manual change made in the console
questions.explanation: A manual change outside code is drift. Regular plans (or GitOps reconciliation) detect it; you then re-apply or update the code to match intent.

questions.prompt: Your app runs on VMs in a single availability zone, and that zone loses power. What design would have kept it running?
options: Bigger instance types in the same zone so each VM can absorb more traffic
Moving from object storage to block storage for all the application data
Running instances across two or three zones behind a load balancer
Disabling autoscaling so the instance count stays fixed during failures
questions.explanation: Availability zones are isolated data centers within a region. Spreading instances across zones behind a load balancer survives a single-zone failure.

questions.prompt: A batch job only needs to read files from one storage bucket. Which permission setup follows least privilege?
options: An admin role, so the job never fails when it later needs extra permissions
A role allowing s3:GetObject on that bucket's objects, with short-lived credentials
A long-lived access key for a personal user account that already has bucket access
A policy with Action "s3:*" on all buckets, limited by a strong password instead
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the needed action on the needed resource. Roles with short-lived credentials avoid leaked long-lived keys and broad wildcards.

questions.prompt: You run a managed SQL database service. Under the shared responsibility model, which task is still yours?
options: Replacing failed disks in the physical servers that host the database instances
Patching the hypervisor that isolates your database from other customers' VMs
Securing the data center building and controlling physical access to the racks
Configuring who can connect: network rules, database users and IAM permissions
questions.explanation: The provider secures the cloud itself (hardware, facilities, hypervisor); you remain responsible for access configuration and your data, even on managed services.
